title: CIL: a stack machine language
sub: Run CIL with your own hands
cards/0/title: CIL: instructions for an imaginary machine
cards/0/body:
CIL (Common Intermediate Language) is a set of simple instructions. They work with a stack, a pile of numbers.

Picture a stack of plates: an instruction puts a number on top or takes the top one off. You can only take from the top.
cards/0/deep: The stack model keeps compilers and code verification simple: nobody has to allocate registers. The JIT does that later for the specific CPU. x64 has 16 general-purpose registers, ARM64 has 31.
cards/1/body: Here is what the compiler turns a + b into. Comments follow //.
cards/1/code:
ldarg.0   // push argument a
ldarg.1   // push argument b
add       // pop two numbers, push their sum
ret       // return whatever is on top
cards/2/task: Press "Step" until the method returns a result. Watch the stack.
cards/3/q: a = 40, b = 2. What is on top of the stack right after ldarg.1?
cards/3/explain: ldarg.1 pushed b = 2 on top of 40. The addition only happens at the next instruction.
cards/3/wrong/1: 40 is underneath: ldarg.0 pushed it, then 2 went on top.
cards/3/wrong/2: 42 only appears after add, and that hasn't run yet.
cards/4/q: Build the CIL for return a * b + c;
cards/4/explain: Push a and b, mul gives a·b, push c, add sums them. The instruction order follows the order of evaluation.
cards/5/task: Let's test your solution on the machine: a = 5, b = 8, c = 2.
cards/6/q: Which instructions does CIL have? Select all that apply.
cards/6/explain: CIL has loads and stores, calls, arithmetic, branches and exceptions. Windows and networking are libraries that are themselves built from such instructions.
cards/7/task: Now a broken program. Press "Step" and see what happens.
cards/8/options/0: add needs two numbers, but the stack has one
cards/8/explain: This CIL is invalid: the stack runs dry (stack underflow). In the safety lesson we'll see who catches errors like this.
cards/9/q: CIL doesn't depend on the CPU. What does that give us?
cards/9/options/0: The same CIL becomes machine code for any supported CPU
cards/9/options/1: CIL runs faster than machine code
cards/9/options/2: CIL doesn't need to be compiled
cards/9/explain: .NET has a JIT compiler for each CPU, while the CIL is shared by all of them.
cards/9/wrong/1: The opposite: the CPU doesn't understand CIL, so it still has to be translated to machine code.
